title: Exa vs TinyFish: What a Three-Page Web Extraction Test Revealed
description: We ran both connected tools on three live pages and checked prices, scope, dates and links. See the observed mismatches, saved outputs and reusable checklist.
quickAnswer: In this single run, TinyFish preserved the current $497 Growth Fix offer and useful download and organizer links. Exa returned a superseded $997 offer and omitted some needed links. TinyFish also dropped package-name headings on one page, so source checks remained necessary.
bodyHtml:
A web extract can look complete while missing the detail your next action depends on. We tested Exa and TinyFish through their connected extraction tools on the same three public pages, then checked their responses against separately retrieved live HTML. One response returned a retired price and scope. Another preserved current prices but dropped the package-name headings.

The practical question was simple: could we use each returned result to describe an offer, share a free sample, or help someone register for an event?

The task and checks were written first

The run began on November 14, 2026 at 00:49 UTC. We chose three pages we publish, so we could inspect the source directly: a digital-product service page, a private Growth Fix offer, and a local event roundup. The checklist required prices paired with scope, useful download or organizer links, preserved dates, and no invented conversion results or free-admission claims.

Each provider received one batch containing the same three URLs. Exa used a 20,000-character extraction limit. TinyFish requested Markdown with links and metadata, with images and iframes excluded and a 45-second limit per URL. These interfaces have different settings; this is an observed workflow comparison, not a controlled comparison of their internal systems.

What each tool actually returned

Page and required resultExa responseTinyFish response
Wealth Experiment: package prices, installment terms and both sample downloads.Preserved the named $497 plan and $1,497 sprint with three $499 payments. Omitted the newly added sample section and both download destinations.Preserved the prices, installment terms and sample text. Both download URLs appeared in the links array. The exact package-name headings were absent from the extracted text.
Agency Growth Fix: current private-service price, three-fix scope and separate workshop.Returned the superseded $997 offer with one implemented improvement. The current $497 service and separate $97 workshop distinction were absent.Returned the current $497 private service, three implemented fixes and separate $97 group workshop.
SouthFLAI: roundup window and upcoming events with usable organizer URLs.Preserved the November 12–18 window and upcoming event dates. The returned text did not include organizer destination URLs.Preserved the window and upcoming event dates. Organizer URLs were available separately in the links array; they still needed to be matched to the relevant event.

Neither response reported a measured conversion increase for our new sample or guided intake. Neither described the library class as free when its fee was not stated. Those checks matter, but they do not cancel a wrong price or a missing registration link.

The price discrepancy was the consequential finding

At the time of our independent check, the live Growth Fix page offered three focused improvements for $497. Exa’s returned text described one improvement for $997. An assistant using that extract without verification could quote the wrong offer.

This establishes a mismatch in this response. It does not establish why the mismatch occurred. The response did not expose a cache timestamp or enough retrieval details to distinguish caching, extraction behavior or another cause. We did not run a second configuration or request a refresh.

A current number still needs its label

On the digital-product page, TinyFish returned the new sample and usable file URLs. It also preserved $497 and $1,497 with the installment terms, but omitted the exact “Product & Audience Plan” and “Build & Launch Sprint” headings from its text. The surrounding descriptions helped, yet a precise product comparison still needed a source check.

Exa preserved those names and prices, but missed the sample. There was no single response that removed the need to review this page. This is why our checklist asks for a fact together with its label and destination, rather than counting words extracted.

Keep a link check in the event workflow

Both outputs included the roundup’s date window and upcoming November 16 and 18 events. TinyFish’s separate links array included the organizer destinations. Exa’s returned text named the events but did not contain those destination URLs.

For a calendar assistant, recognizing an event is only part of the job. A usable result also needs the correct registration destination and the organizer’s current attendance terms. Check those before sending an invitation or telling someone to travel.

What we would use next

For this three-page task, TinyFish supplied more of the current information and destination links needed to continue. We would still check package labels and map links to events. Exa’s response needed a new source check for the offer price and additional retrieval for the sample and organizer URLs.

We have not established a universal winner. This was one batch per provider, using publisher-owned pages. We did not measure billed cost, repeatability, full review time or performance across unrelated sites. A continuing workflow should repeat the important cases on another day and include external pages before choosing a default.

Inspect the outputs. Repeat the test.

Download the original responses and source-check record. The JSON includes the prewritten criteria, configuration notes, returned text and links, independently captured source text, and the limits of this run. Get the reusable extraction checklist for your own pages.

Use the tool-trial planner to define a task and acceptance checks. Our ten-tool field guide offers other trial ideas; this article supplies a separate, completed extraction example. The products in that shortlist were not tested as part of this run.

title: llms.txt vs APIs vs MCP: An Agent-Ready Website Guide
description: An implementation guide to agent-friendly websites, with a short llms.txt template, API contract, failure tests and a practical decision framework.
quickAnswer: The Route Doctor newsletter example describes a short llms.txt file and two public endpoints, with a successful Claude test reported by its author. That is an instructive pattern, not evidence that every agent will discover the file or that the approach improves rankings. The linked project and checker could not be independently verified during this review, so this guide does not repeat their commands as tested installation instructions.
bodyHtml:
Use this guide

  • Worked example: a service lookup contract
  • The six-step implementation
  • A short llms.txt you can adapt
  • A better audit prompt
  • Test what happened, not what the assistant says happened

There is a useful idea inside the excitement about agent-ready websites: stop making software infer every capability from a visually complex page. Give it a short map, a clear contract and a result it can check. The mistake is treating those ingredients as a universal certification or a shortcut to search rankings.

The practical answer

The Route Doctor newsletter example describes a short llms.txt file and two public endpoints, with a successful Claude test reported by its author. That is an instructive pattern, not evidence that every agent will discover the file or that the approach improves rankings. The linked project and checker could not be independently verified during this review, so this guide does not repeat their commands as tested installation instructions.

What to build—and what each layer does

LayerUseful jobWhat it does not establish
Readable, accessible pagesExplain the offer and make the next action understandable.That an agent will interpret every detail correctly.
A short llms.txtProvide a concise map for clients that use it.Permission, universal adoption or a search ranking boost.
Documented read-only dataReturn structured facts for a defined task.That those facts are fresh or safe without maintenance.
Optional MCP integrationExpose capabilities to compatible clients.Automatic discovery, authorization or reliable outcomes.

Choose the layer that solves the observed problem. llms.txt proposal and format describes the file convention; OpenAPI specification describes HTTP API contracts; Model Context Protocol architecture explains MCP’s client/server architecture. These are different responsibilities.

Choose the lightest useful interface

If the task is reading information, a well-structured page may suffice. If the task is retrieving fresh, structured data, a documented read-only API can reduce ambiguity. OpenAPI describes the HTTP contract; it does not run the service. MCP connects compatible clients to exposed capabilities and introduces its own implementation and maintenance work. Add it when a real client workflow benefits. None of these automatically grants the agent permissions.

Worked example: a service lookup contract

Use a fixed public service catalog for the first prototype. GET /api/v1/services returns identifiers, names, scope, pricing basis, source URLs and a checked date. A query for an unsupported identifier returns an explicit error, not an empty success message or invented match. Unknown routes return 404; unsupported methods return 405. Keep the example free of customer data and administrative actions.

Test the contract beyond the happy path

Validate both status and content type. A 200 response containing your application’s HTML shell is not a valid JSON API response. Check malformed input, no matching result, rate limiting, stale data and upstream failure. If a request is retried, ensure it does not create a duplicate action. For real deployments, add appropriate authorization, abuse controls, operational logs and ownership; a documentation file is not a security boundary.

The six-step implementation

  1. Define the task. Choose one safe useful action.
  2. Write the contract. Inputs, outputs and errors.
  3. Implement the read. Keep private data out.
  4. Publish the map. Link real docs and endpoints.
  5. Test failure paths. Verify status and response.
  6. Observe real use. Maintain what clients need.

A short llms.txt you can adapt

This is an illustrative template. Replace every example.com URL with an existing public page on your own domain. Check the content, not just the link. If your site has no public API, leave API instructions out. Do not publish placeholder endpoints, private URLs, access tokens or customer information.

# Service Finder Demo

> Discover a documented read-only service, call it with valid input, and explain an error without inventing a result.

## Useful pages
- [Main information](https://example.com/docs/): The current offering and relevant details.
- [Conditions and process](https://example.com/api-reference/): Eligibility, limitations and how the process works.
- [Next step](https://example.com/status/): The official route for a person to continue.

## Boundaries
This example does not support automated purchases or bookings.
Use the linked pages for current facts; ask when information is missing.

Serve the file at your site root when your hosting setup supports it. In a typical static build, that means placing it in the directory copied to the public root. Verify the deployed URL: a local file alone is not a published file. If your platform already generates one, inspect and maintain that version instead of creating conflicting instructions.

If you need an API, start with a read

The following is a proposed contract, not an endpoint installed on this site. Choose fields that answer the task, document their types and meaning, and return only information you intend to make public. Include a source URL and an update signal where useful. A checked date records a review; it does not guarantee the underlying data is current.

GET https://example.com/api/v1/services
Accept: application/json

{
  "example": true,
  "checked_at": "2026-11-11",
  "items": [{
    "id": "intro",
    "name": "Introductory service",
    "pricing_basis": "Request a current quote",
    "source_url": "https://example.com/services/",
    "available_actions": ["read_details"]
  }]
}

Define no-result and error behavior as carefully as success. Keep private data behind proper access controls. For future actions that change records or spend money, design authentication, authorization, explicit confirmation and duplicate-action protection separately. OWASP API Security Project provides a useful security review starting point.

A better audit prompt

Use an assistant with browsing or request capabilities. If it cannot access the site, it should report the limitation; a fluent response is not proof of inspection.

Review this public website: [URL]. Task: Discover a documented read-only service, call it with valid input, and explain an error without inventing a result.

Use browsing or request tools if available; if unavailable, say what you cannot verify. Inspect the relevant public pages and /llms.txt. Record the URLs you actually fetched and the facts you found. Do not infer success from a 200 response alone. Separate observed facts, missing information and suggested changes. Do not sign in, submit forms, change data, add to a cart or purchase.

Draft a concise llms.txt using only verified public URLs. Include an API example only if a documented public endpoint exists and its read operation is appropriate to test. Do not invent endpoints. Rank the three most useful fixes by customer impact and effort. Explain how to retest each one.

Test what happened, not what the assistant says happened

TestEvidence to keepA passing result
Retrieve the mapFinal URL, status, content type and response body.The actual text file appears; no login page or application shell.
Follow its linksThe final destination and the relevant source facts.Useful pages resolve and match the stated purpose.
Try the customer taskExact prompt, tool capability, answer and cited URLs.Required facts and next step are correct.
Ask an unsupported questionThe answer and what the source actually says.The assistant names the limit rather than inventing a capability.
Repeat after a changeSource version, date and all attempted runs.Any improvement is reproducible within the tested setup.

Measure for this site’s use case: Contract-valid responses, factual task completion, error recovery, latency and maintenance burden. Tool adoption and rankings require separate evidence.

Run a baseline before editing. Use fresh sessions and keep the prompt and available tools comparable. Include failed attempts in your denominator. Record whether you explicitly told the agent about llms.txt; that is different from observing spontaneous discovery. A scanner is a diagnostic aid, not a certification.

Avoid the shortcuts that create new problems

  • Do not replace readable pages with machine-only content. People still need to evaluate the offer.
  • Do not treat robots.txt or llms.txt as authentication. Protect private routes with real access controls.
  • Do not tell every crawler it may access everything merely to improve a score.
  • Do not duplicate prices and policies into several files without an update process.
  • Do not claim a successful booking, lead or sale from a generated answer. Verify the actual system result.

For interface implementation, consult Google web.dev: agent-friendly website UX and W3C: labeling form controls. Preserve descriptive controls, meaningful form labels and visible state changes. Agent testing complements human usability and accessibility testing.

Questions worth answering

Will llms.txt improve Google rankings?

No ranking benefit is established by adding this file. Google’s current guidance says it does not use llms.txt for Search visibility. Treat the file as an optional usability aid for clients that consume it; keep ordinary SEO work and task testing separate.

Do I need MCP or Markdown copies of every page?

Not for every project. Start with the smallest interface the task requires. Add Markdown resources or a compatible tool integration when there is a clear consumer and maintenance plan. Check platform support rather than assuming all assistants behave the same way.

Can I use this without coding?

Yes. You can clarify public pages, check links and run the task exercise with your existing website editor and assistant. Publishing a root file depends on the host. A public API requires additional implementation; ask for help if that is outside your skills.

How often should I review it?

Review whenever an offering, policy, route or API contract changes. Assign an owner. Frequently changing prices or stock need stronger freshness controls than a static guide.

Search guidance: Google Search: optimizing for generative AI. Documentation reviewed November 11, 2026. Provider behavior can change; recheck the linked sources when implementing.

Optional hosting for a working prototype

Your existing host may be sufficient. If a custom read-only service needs deployment, you can evaluate Railway through our referral link. Compare current usage charges and operating requirements before choosing it. Referral disclosure: we may receive a benefit for qualifying activity. No paid host is required to complete the planning and local test exercises.

Put one improvement to work

Start with this task: Discover a documented read-only service, call it with valid input, and explain an error without inventing a result. Save the baseline, make one justified improvement and keep the retest evidence. Use the result to choose the next useful change.

Plan a useful tool trial →

Sources and editorial notes

  • llms.txt proposal and format
  • Google Search: optimizing for generative AI
  • Google web.dev: agent-friendly website UX
  • W3C: labeling form controls
  • OpenAPI specification
  • Model Context Protocol architecture
  • OWASP API Security Project

This guide combines primary-source documentation with original implementation advice and a fictional worked example. It is not a report of measured client results, guaranteed traffic or earnings. The examples use reserved example.com URLs and must be adapted and verified before deployment.

Continue with the right practical resource

Choose the resource that matches the job you are doing.

  • Compare AI tools by the task — Choose the job and evaluation criteria before selecting software.
  • Plan a tool trial — Define one result to test with an existing tool.
  • Use the classroom implementation checklist — AI Teachers provides a repeatable practice sequence.

title: Agent harnesses and inference: choose an AI tool for the whole job
description: Compare the model's output, connected tools, saved results, and recovery on one small task before choosing an AI environment.
answerQuestion: How do inference and an agent harness affect the AI tool I choose?
quickAnswer: Inference produces the model's next output. The harness manages the session, context, tools, and continuing work around it. Compare both by asking each tool to finish the same small job, then inspect the actual deliverable and your total review effort.
bodyHtml:
A useful AI tool has to fit the whole job you want to finish. You may need a good answer, a saved document, information from a connected app, or several steps that continue after an interruption. Two terms help you ask better questions about that fit: inference and the agent harness.

This guide turns those terms into a small comparison you can run yourself. The exercise uses fictional meeting notes and one action brief. It builds on our AI terms for tool buyers and the guide to prompts and agent workflows, with a closer look at what happens between a request and a finished result.

Inference is what the model does with its current input

During inference, a trained model processes input and produces output. For a language model, that output can include prose, code, or a structured request to use a tool. Ordinary inference uses the model's trained weights; it does not retrain those weights for every assignment. Cloudflare's glossary defines the term, and its inference and training explainer describes the distinction.

In our exercise, the model reads the meeting notes and proposes an action brief. Its output might identify a missing owner or notice that two deadlines conflict. Those are things you can check directly against the supplied notes.

The harness manages the session around the model

The harness is the software coordinating the work: assembling context, calling the model, routing permitted tool requests, returning results, and maintaining the session. Microsoft's explanation of agent harnesses describes that loop.

If the agent requests a file, a connected tool performs the operation and returns a result. The next model call can use that result. A single assignment may therefore involve several inference calls and tool operations.

The exact capabilities depend on the environment. Check which files, apps, permissions, progress records, and limits are actually available. A product's use of the word “agent” does not tell you which of those features your account has.

Choose one small job for your comparison

Imagine you need an action brief from a short meeting. Create a fictional sample with five notes: two clearly assigned tasks, one task with no owner, one unresolved decision, and one task described with conflicting deadlines. Avoid real private meeting material while learning the process.

Define the output before trying either tool: a table containing task, owner, deadline, source note, and unresolved question, followed by a short summary. Missing owners must stay unassigned, conflicting dates must remain visible, and no decision may be presented as agreed unless the notes say so.

If saving an editable file is part of your real workflow, make that an explicit requirement. A good brief displayed in a chat and an editable brief saved to the correct location are different observations to record.

Inspect the answer and the completed work

LayerQuestion for this trialEvidence to keep
Model outputDoes the brief accurately represent the notes?The brief and a check against each source note.
ContextDid the session use the right version of the notes?The input filename or version supplied.
ToolsDid the requested file operation succeed?An editable file you can open at the intended location.
RecoveryWhat happens when a required step cannot finish?The reported problem and any completed work preserved.
ReviewCan you identify and correct an error efficiently?Your corrections and time spent reviewing.

These checks help you locate a problem. An invented owner points to an output that needs correction. An accurate brief that was never saved points to a different gap in the workflow. Both matter when the requested deliverable is a saved, usable document.

Anthropic's agent evaluation guidance distinguishes the record of an agent's actions from the resulting state of the environment. Apply that distinction by opening the file and checking its contents, rather than relying only on a completion message.

Use the same brief in each environment

Create an action brief from these fictional meeting notes. Include task, owner, deadline, source note, and unresolved question. Keep missing facts and conflicting statements visible. Use only the supplied notes for meeting facts. Save an editable result to [permitted location] if that capability is available; otherwise explain what output you can provide. Return the brief, its location, the checks performed, and unresolved items. Do not send the brief or update anyone's tasks.

Keep the inputs and acceptance criteria consistent. Record the product, date, relevant settings, enabled tools, and model name when the product exposes it. Two applications can use a similar underlying model while giving it different context and tools, so a difference in results does not isolate the cause by itself.

This is a workflow comparison for your task. It does not establish a general ranking of the underlying models.

Try one revision and one interruption

After the first brief, supply a corrected deadline and ask for an updated version. Check that the correction appears in the actual deliverable and that unrelated tasks remain intact.

For a second practice run, leave out an input the task requires, or use a test destination that is deliberately unavailable. Observe whether the agent reports the problem accurately, preserves useful work, and identifies what is needed to continue. Keep this exercise inside an environment you control.

If your workflow depends on resuming later, test that separately. Reopening a chat is not evidence that the system retained every file, permission, or task state needed to finish the job.

Compare total effort before choosing

Record preparation, hands-on work, review, corrections, and any recovery effort. Track elapsed time separately, including time spent waiting. Record usage or cost when the product makes it available; bundled subscriptions and usage-based tools may present that information differently.

More inference calls can add opportunities to check and revise, but they also consume time and resources. Let the accepted result determine whether the extra work was worthwhile. Repeat the trial on another sample before making a larger commitment.

Use the Tool Trial Lab to record your observations. Choose the environment that gives you an acceptable deliverable with manageable effort, appropriate access, and a clear way to recover. The practical value of understanding inference and the harness is knowing what to inspect before you rely on the workflow.

title: Give agents the work: six ways to finish more of what matters
description: Turn research, reporting, forms, content and product work into finished deliverables—with briefs, copyable prompts and a practical quality scorecard.
answerQuestion: Give agents the work: six ways to finish more of what matters
quickAnswer: Give an agent a bounded job, approved inputs, an output format and a definition of done. Start with one workflow, check its result, and measure your total effort before expanding.
bodyHtml:
There is a satisfying difference between getting an answer and crossing something off your list. An agent workflow aims for the second: gather the relevant material, do the work, create a usable result and show what happened. The opportunity is more finished work with less repetitive handling. Whether it actually saves time depends on the task and the review it needs.

These are original practice workflows, not independently benchmarked performance claims. Choose an agent you can already access. For setup, see our Grok Bot, Claude Desktop and ChatGPT Work guides.

Start with a brief the agent can finish

A useful brief answers five questions: What will exist when the task is done? Which inputs are authoritative? What may the agent change? What should happen when something is missing? How will you check the result? Give it a small first batch so you can correct the method before repeating mistakes across a hundred records.

Outcome: create [deliverable] for [audience].
Use: [files, URLs, approved accounts and date range].
Include: [required fields, format and quality criteria].
If information is missing, label it and ask only what blocks the task.
You may: [allowed actions]. Stop before: [external action].
Return the result, sources, unresolved issues and a completion checklist.

Six jobs worth trying

1. Research that becomes a decision

Choose a real purchasing or project question. Supply five candidate vendors and three non-negotiable requirements. Request a comparison with source URLs, dates and unknowns, then a one-page recommendation. The finished result is a decision aid rather than a pile of links.

Compare these five providers against our requirements. Use official pages.
Create a table with evidence for each criterion. Mark unverified claims.
Recommend two to investigate, explaining the tradeoffs. Do not contact them.

2. A recurring report that leads to action

Provide two small approved exports with matching periods. Ask the agent to reconcile totals, calculate changes and produce three questions for your review. With fictional data, 40 inquiries and 10 bookings means a 25% inquiry-to-booking rate. A report that calls that a 10% rate needs correction before automation.

Check these exports for missing dates and duplicate rows. Calculate the
agreed metrics with visible formulas. Create a brief separating observed
changes from possible explanations. Do not change campaigns or budgets.

3. Forms prepared from one reliable profile

Use a harmless test form you control and a short approved business profile. Have the agent map every field to supplied information, fill the available fields, and list gaps. Review the complete form before authorizing submission. Check which actions actually persist: some forms save while you type.

Prepare this test form using only my approved profile. Leave unsupported
answers blank. Show the field-to-source mapping and stop before submission,
terms acceptance or any payment. Report any automatic save behavior.

4. One good source becomes a content package

Supply a source article you own, approved claims, audience and offer. Ask for an email, a social post and a six-slide outline with a consistent call to action. Compare every factual statement against the source; remove invented quotes, customer outcomes and statistics.

Turn this approved article into three formats. Preserve its meaning.
Give each format a distinct opening. Add a claim checklist with source
locations. Save editable drafts; publication is a separate decision.

5. Feedback becomes a product review

Give the agent anonymized feedback, current constraints and the question the team must decide. Ask for themes, contradictory evidence, example quotes and candidate experiments. Frequency in a small sample is not proof of market demand, and a request is not automatically a roadmap commitment.

Group this feedback by user problem. Retain record IDs, conflicting
examples and uncertainty. Suggest three small experiments with success
criteria. Do not invent customers, research findings or priority scores.

6. A web page gets a useful quality review

Choose one public page or your own test environment. Ask the agent to follow the primary journey and record broken links, confusing instructions and missing states. Request findings with reproduction steps. A concrete issue such as an unlabeled required field is more useful than “improve the UX.”

Review this page on desktop and a narrow mobile viewport if supported.
Test navigation and the primary task without sending real inquiries.
Return evidence, severity, reproduction steps and proposed fixes.

Give each tool a job

A connected app can supply structured records; a browser handles visible website interactions; file tools create deliverables. OpenAI's plugin documentation explains how installed plugins bring skills and service tools into Work. Pick the smallest access that completes your task. Several agents only help when their assignments and handoffs are clear; one person should own the final acceptance decision.

Measure finished work, including the cleanup

MeasureRecord after each run
QualityRequired facts correct, missing items, corrections needed
Your timeBriefing + monitoring + review + repair
Elapsed timeStart to accepted deliverable, including interruptions
CostRelevant subscription or usage cost
DecisionKeep, revise or stop—with the reason

Compare against how you normally do the same work. Save an accepted example and test the method on a fresh input. Only then turn the process into a reusable skill; OpenAI documents skill creation, and Grok Bot documents skills and routines. Scheduling needs its own owner, timezone and failure behavior.

Pick one job for this week. The win is a reliable result you would use again. Try the Tool Trial Lab, or bring your process to a $350 AI Working Session.

title: Grok Bot: your first useful teammate, from setup to a finished task
description: Set up one focused Bot, complete a source-linked research brief, and turn an accepted result into a reusable routine.
answerQuestion: Grok Bot: your first useful teammate, from setup to a finished task
quickAnswer: Start with the official Grok Bot app and an eligible account. Give one Bot a clear responsibility, run a small task, inspect the output, and save the method only after it works.
bodyHtml:
A useful first Grok Bot does not need to run your whole business. Give it a job you already understand: a weekly research brief, a draft reporting pack, or a tidy set of project notes. You will learn more from one finished task than from creating a large team before anyone has an assignment.

This guide covers the official Grok Bot product. It is distinct from regular Grok chat and unrelated projects using the GrokBot name. The exercises below are our suggested workflows, not independent benchmarks or a promise of unattended accuracy.

1. Get into the right app

Use the official getting-started page to check eligibility and download the app. Current access includes multiple paid X, Cursor and Grok routes; check your existing entitlement before buying another subscription. Desktop builds cover macOS, Windows and Linux, with mobile options also documented.

Follow the account sign-in flow for your entitlement. After onboarding, use the sidebar's plus control to create a Bot, choose a name and give it one main responsibility. Account and menu details can change, so use the linked documentation when your screen differs.

2. Give the Bot a job, not a personality alone

A name makes the Bot easy to find; a role makes it useful. For a first example, create “Research Desk.” Give it a narrow remit and an output you can evaluate without connecting private business systems.

Your job is to prepare short research briefs from public official sources.
For each claim, retain the source URL and date checked.
Separate verified facts, your interpretation and unanswered questions.
Return a comparison table and a one-page brief.
Do not contact companies, register accounts, buy anything or publish.
Remember this working method for future research tasks.

Ask it to restate the job in its own words. Correct any expansion of scope before supplying the first assignment. “Research software” is broad; “compare these three providers against these four requirements” has a finish line.

3. Complete one small research brief

Choose three tools you are considering and four requirements that matter to your work. For example: export format, collaboration, available integrations and account requirements. Do not ask the Bot to invent a numerical ranking when some facts are missing.

Research these three provider URLs: [paste URLs].
Compare these requirements: [paste four requirements].
Use official product or help pages and show a source beside each fact.
Mark missing or ambiguous information as unknown.
Create an editable comparison and a brief recommending my next two checks.
Finish in this conversation. No outreach or purchases.

Open a few source links yourself. Check whether the quoted capability belongs to the correct product and plan. An accessible marketing page is not proof that your account has the feature. Ask the Bot to revise any unsupported conclusion, then keep the corrected deliverable as the example for next time.

4. Understand the computer your Bots use

Grok Bot's computer documentation describes a persistent cloud environment. Bots on your account share files, logins and credentials; different Bot roles do not create separate security compartments. Open the conversation's computer preview to inspect the work. For authentication, use the secure form or take-over flow instead of pasting passwords into chat.

When a supported connected app can do the job, connect that app deliberately and review its access. Add one source at a time. For this first research exercise, public URLs should be enough. A later reporting workflow can use approved exports before it needs access to your live analytics account.

5. Try a reporting job with an expected answer

Use our existing Weekly Growth Decision Brief template kit. It includes fictional sample resources, a suggested setup and evaluation materials. Start with those samples, then compare the output with the expected brief. A template is a starting method; it does not establish that future runs will be correct.

Add one deliberate problem: remove a reporting date, duplicate a row, or leave bookings blank. A useful Bot flags the issue and explains which conclusions it cannot support. It should not silently treat missing bookings as zero or compare different reporting periods.

Use the fictional sample only. Show the calculation behind each metric.
Identify missing periods, duplicates and zero denominators.
Distinguish an observed change from a possible cause.
Recommend three checks, and keep all account changes as proposals.

6. Save the method, then decide about scheduling

Once you have an accepted run, ask the Bot to save the process as a skill. Skills capture the method; routines determine when a Bot runs it. Review the saved instructions and test a fresh sample before creating a recurring job.

Save this accepted workflow as a skill called Research Decision Brief.
Include the required inputs, source checks, output structure and stop rules.
Read the saved method back to me. Do not schedule it yet.

For a later routine, specify an owner, timezone, approved inputs, delivery destination and what to do when a source is unavailable. Ask it to report a failed run rather than recycle stale information as new. Verify the routine exists and inspect its first actual run.

Know what you are approving

Grok Bot's approval system considers your request and custom rules. Read the actual operation and destination before approving a consequential action. If a request is unclear, ask for a draft or a before-and-after view. Finish your first session with one checked deliverable and one reusable method. That is enough to build on.

title: Let Claude Desktop do the clicking: a practical computer-use guide
description: Enable computer use, choose the right access, and turn a small desktop task into a checked file or completed workflow.
answerQuestion: Let Claude Desktop do the clicking: a practical computer-use guide
quickAnswer: In eligible Claude Desktop accounts, enable computer use in settings and ask for a bounded task. Approve the apps it needs, watch the first run, and inspect the actual output.
bodyHtml:
That repetitive sequence of opening a page, copying details and turning them into a document is a good place to test an agent. Claude Desktop can help carry out work as well as discuss it. The useful question is what you want finished, which information it may use, and how you will know the result is right.

This guide separates direct desktop control from browser work and connected apps. The exercises are original examples to try with your own approved material. We have not independently benchmarked these workflows or measured a universal time-saving result.

Check availability, then enable computer use

According to Anthropic's computer-use guide, the beta is available in Claude Desktop on macOS and Windows for Pro, Max and Ultra. Team and Enterprise do not currently have this direct computer-use capability. Cowork access alone does not mean every control feature is enabled.

  1. Update Claude Desktop from the official download page.
  2. Open Settings → Capabilities; if the section is absent, look under Settings → System → This computer.
  3. Turn on Enable computer use.
  4. Start a Cowork or Claude Code session. Some accounts have a unified Chat/Cowork interface.
  5. Describe a small task and approve the specific applications requested.

Keep your computer awake and Claude Desktop open. Direct screen interaction can make mistakes and is often slower than a connector. Use a connector when it covers the job; reserve desktop control for work that needs the screen.

Choose the route that fits the task

RouteGood first taskWhat to inspect
Connected appRead one approved document or projectThe account, accessible records and allowed actions
Built-in browserReview public pages and prepare a comparisonThe URLs and facts used
Desktop computer useInspect a practice app without a connectorThe permitted app and visible changes

The built-in browser opens in Claude Desktop's side panel and is separate from your everyday browser. Claude in Chrome is a different option that works through the extension in your Chrome browser. The built-in browser also depends on Desktop staying open and online. Choose the environment deliberately when existing tabs or sign-ins matter.

Practice task: turn public pages into an event brief

Pick three public event pages from organizers. Your goal is an editable comparison for a team learning day, containing date, timezone, venue, registration link and unresolved details. This task is easy to inspect and does not require registering anyone.

Use these three official event pages: [URLs].
Create an editable event comparison and a one-page recommendation.
Record the date, timezone, location, registration link and date checked.
Mark absent details as unknown. Exclude events before [date].
Use the browser if needed. Do not register, pay, send or publish.
Show which sources support the final recommendation.

Review the first extracted event before asking for the rest. Confirm that the year is correct and that “virtual” does not mean a local venue. Ask Claude to show any conflicting dates. Your acceptance criteria should include a real output file, working links and a clear explanation of what remains unknown.

Practice task: inspect a desktop workflow

Use a practice application or a copy of a project you own. Choose a short journey such as opening a sample file, finding a setting and documenting the steps. Start with observation; a complete set of reproduction steps is useful even before you authorize a fix.

In [approved practice app], inspect how a new user opens [sample file]
and reaches [specific setting]. Record the exact steps and any confusion.
Create a short illustrated instruction sheet if screenshots are supported.
Do not change preferences, delete files or touch other applications.
If the screen differs from the expected state, stop and describe it.

Watch the first run. Verify that screenshots contain only the practice content and that the instructions match the application version. A generated instruction sheet should distinguish actions Claude performed from suggestions it has not tried.

Move from observation to a small change

After the inspection succeeds, choose one reversible action in a duplicate file. For example, ask Claude to format a copied agenda with heading styles and a clear action table, saving it under a new name. Supply the desired filename and folder. Ask for the output location and a short list of changes.

Use the copy named Practice Agenda. Apply consistent heading styles
and arrange the supplied actions into owner, task and due-date columns.
Keep every original fact. Save as Practice Agenda - Formatted.
Do not overwrite the source. Open the saved result and check it.

Verify that the output opens, all actions survived, and no deadline appeared without a source. Compare total time spent directing and correcting the work with the time you normally spend. Keep a successful example for future tasks.

Make the next run easier to review

Anthropic's Cowork guidance explains that access determines what an agent can read and change. Use a practice folder and approved apps, close unrelated sensitive material, and inspect unexpected requests. Direct computer use interacts with real applications; a written stop rule is useful but is not an isolation boundary.

If a task stalls, narrow it to one page or one file and state the expected screen. If a connector is available, consider that route. Keep the accepted input, prompt, output and corrections together. Your next improvement should remove a repeated source of confusion, not simply ask Claude to “be better.” Continue with the six practical agent jobs or bring a task to a working session.

title: ChatGPT Work: research the web, prepare forms and create the deliverables
description: A practical Work guide for turning approved sources and web tasks into checked spreadsheets, briefs and ready-to-review forms.
answerQuestion: ChatGPT Work: research the web, prepare forms and create the deliverables
quickAnswer: Start a Work task with a clear deliverable, source URLs and action boundaries. Use available plugins or browser tools, review extracted data and forms, and verify the saved result.
bodyHtml:
Imagine finishing a research task with the spreadsheet, the decision brief and the next-step draft already prepared. That is a useful way to approach ChatGPT Work: describe the work product and the checks it needs, then give it the context and access to complete the steps.

The following exercises are original suggested workflows. They are not independently tested speed comparisons. The aim is to reduce repeated handling while keeping the result accurate enough to use.

Start a Work task with a finish line

Open Work in ChatGPT and describe the output. For web tasks, OpenAI documents a cloud browser that runs separately from your device's browser. It does not inherit your local tabs or sign-ins. Website access depends on plan, rollout and workspace controls; authenticated browsing is currently documented for Plus and Pro on web/mobile, not Enterprise or Edu.

Approve relevant site access when prompted. Use the provided secure sign-in flow rather than putting credentials in chat. The agent can read, click and type on supported sites; some sites block automation or need a human step. Review consequential submissions and payments when prompted.

Connect the source when a plugin can do the job

For work in a supported service, open Plugins, inspect the relevant plugin and connect the intended account when prompted. Start a new chat after installation. You can name the plugin with @ or describe the task. OpenAI's plugin guide distinguishes reusable skills from tools that read or act in connected services.

Choose the source of truth before starting. If the approved event dates are in one document, specify that document. If the task needs current public pricing, require the provider's official page. Access to a service is not proof that every needed action is supported; ask Work to identify missing capabilities rather than pretending a step finished.

Workflow 1: pull public data into a usable spreadsheet

Choose five to ten official event pages. Define the columns, date range and rule for missing information. Request both the dataset and a short note explaining exclusions. This creates a file you can filter and update rather than a long answer you must copy by hand.

Research these official event URLs: [URLs].
Create a spreadsheet with event, organizer, date, timezone, venue,
registration URL, source URL and checked date.
Include only events between [start] and [end]. Do not guess missing values.
Deduplicate by event, date and venue; explain any conflicts.
Return the spreadsheet plus a short summary. Do not register anyone.

Check the row count and inspect at least three rows against their source pages. Confirm that the date columns sort as dates, each registration link belongs to the right event, and recurring events are not collapsed into one date. Ask for a clearly labeled “needs checking” column when evidence is incomplete.

Workflow 2: prepare a form without inventing answers

Start on a test form you control. Provide a short approved business profile and identify the exact form URL. Before filling it, ask Work to inspect which fields are required and whether the site saves entries automatically. That distinction matters: leaving the final button untouched does not always mean nothing was saved.

Use [test form URL] and the approved profile below.
List required fields, then fill only values supported by the profile.
Leave unknown fields blank and show me a field-to-source review.
Do not submit, accept legal terms, upload files or make a payment.
If typing triggers saving, tell me before entering information.

Review names, dates, recipient, checkboxes and optional marketing consent. After you decide to submit, authorize that specific action and ask for the confirmation or receipt. A success message in the conversation is not enough if the page still shows validation errors. File-upload support differs by environment; OpenAI's current browser guide says built-in browser uploads cannot be automated, so keep a manual handoff available.

Workflow 3: create the report from the data

Work supports creating documents, spreadsheets, presentations and PDFs; see OpenAI’s file guide for the available preview and review surfaces.

Continue from the accepted spreadsheet rather than restarting the research. Ask for a one-page recommendation and a short presentation that use the same source facts. Keep the audience, decision and preferred format explicit.

Using only the checked spreadsheet, create a one-page event shortlist
and a six-slide editable presentation for our team learning day.
Show two options, the decision criteria, unresolved questions and next steps.
Use the source links in speaker notes or an appendix.
Do not invent attendance, testimonials, prices or availability.
Check that the files open and that tables fit their pages.

Open the deliverables. Check that the recommendation matches the table and that no chart implies data you never supplied. Review the title, labels and text size. Ask for a revision with precise feedback such as “the date column wraps awkwardly” or “this recommendation ignores the travel limit.”

Keep a completion record

CheckEvidence to request
Research completedSource URLs, checked dates and unresolved gaps
Form preparedField mapping and the actual on-page state
Submission completedConfirmation or receipt after authorized submission
File createdA working file link and a format check

Turn a useful run into a repeatable method

Record your briefing, review and correction time. Compare the accepted result with your normal process. If the method works on another input, use Skill Creator in Work to capture the steps and acceptance checklist. Invoke @skill-creator and supply your accepted example. Review the skill before reuse; a saved method does not itself create a schedule or connect an account.

Start with one modest task that has a visible finish. Then add the next step that removes real work from your list. Explore the tool directory, try the Tool Trial Lab, or get help applying this to your business in a $350 AI Working Session.

title: Find, create and use AI skills: a practical trial guide
description: Choose a skill by the work it helps you finish. Find official catalogs, use Skill Creator, test a realistic example and build workflows with clear handoffs.
quickAnswer: Start with one task and a result you can check. Inspect available skills, test one with your usual inputs, and use Skill Creator when you need to capture your own method. Save the skill in the right product and review a fresh run.
answerQuestion: How do I find and create a useful AI skill?
bodyHtml:
A skill is a reusable method for a task. Choosing one starts with the output you need: a checked action plan, a campaign brief or a product-page review. One method you can inspect and repeat is a useful place to begin.

Know what you are choosing

A prompt describes the current request. A skill packages a reusable process. A connector supplies access to tools or data. A plugin can bundle capabilities for installation. A skill can guide a connected action, but it does not supply credentials or run on a schedule by itself.

The Agent Skills format centers on SKILL.md, with a name, a description and instructions. Optional references, assets and scripts support the job. Check the host’s compatibility and dependencies as well as the file format.

Where to find existing skills

Start with the skills available in your app, then inspect official publisher catalogs. Search by the result you need rather than a broad label such as “productivity.”

  • OpenAI skills catalog: examples and curated skills for Codex. Use the installation route described in its current documentation.
  • Anthropic skills repository: examples, templates and Skill Creator. Check the instructions and license for the particular package.
  • Your product’s directory: look for skills or plugins available to your account and workspace. An installed plugin may include both skills and connected tools.
  • Your own process: a good completed example and a checklist can become the brief for a custom skill.

Before trying one, record its publisher, source, last relevant update, intended host, dependencies and requested access. A downloaded file is not necessarily an installed capability. Do not assume a skill from another host will work unchanged.

A five-step skill trial

Use the Tool Trial Lab to keep your comparison concrete. Write the input once and judge each result against the same criteria.

When to use Skill Creator

Create a skill when your preferred method is clear but no existing option follows it. Capture a process you perform repeatedly and can evaluate yourself.

  1. Show the creator one good input and output.
  2. Describe when the method should and should not apply.
  3. Ask for concise instructions with a clear output format.
  4. Test an ordinary request and two edge cases.
  5. Save or install through your host and select it for a fresh task.

In ChatGPT Work, invoke @skill-creator; in Codex, use $skill-creator. Anthropic publishes a separate Skill Creator implementation for supported Claude environments. Follow the installed package’s invocation instructions.

Create an instruction-only skill named tool-trial-summary.
Use it when I provide two tool trial records for the same job.
Compare correctness, missing facts, review time and required access.
Return a decision with evidence and remaining unknowns.
Do not infer a winner from popularity or invented scores.
Ask for missing trial data. Test a tie, an incomplete record
and a result that is fast but inaccurate. Help me save the skill.

The illustrated AI Teachers walkthrough covers creation, testing and saving.

Worked example: meeting follow-up

Imagine two candidates receive these fictional notes: “Maya will send an outline Friday. A designer was suggested. Budget not agreed.” Candidate A drafts a polished email that assigns the designer and invents a budget. Candidate B leaves those points unresolved. Candidate B preserves the evidence better, even if you still edit its prose.

For the second run, remove the deadline. For the third, add conflicting deadlines. A useful result identifies the gap or conflict. Record what actually happened; do not mark a case as passed because the skill promises to handle it.

RecordWhat to write
Task and inputThe exact job and material supplied.
Expected resultObservable requirements defined before the run.
Actual resultWhat the assistant produced or changed.
Review effortCorrections needed and time spent checking.
DecisionKeep, adapt or remove, with a reason.

Advanced use: references, tools and handoffs

Keep the recurring method in the main instructions and current facts in maintained references. Add templates for stable output formats. Add scripts for exact operations you can test with known inputs.

A connected workflow needs a clear source and authorized tool access. If research, drafting and review use separate skills, specify what passes between them: sources, dates, claims, open questions and the deliverable. Give the reviewer the original evidence. A second assistant’s agreement is not independent verification.

Compare with a baseline, including human correction time. Keep unseen test examples for revisions. Assign an owner and retain a known working version. Sharing and scheduling need separate setup; copying a skill folder does not transfer a signed-in account.

Make one useful choice today

Choose one recurring task, inspect one skill and run one example. Keep it if it improves the result after review; adapt it if the method nearly fits; remove it if setup outweighs the benefit. Continue with the tool test-bench guide or RAG, MCP and agents explainer.

Choose tools by the job they do

This shortlist separates creation, discovery, implementation and connection. These are documented resources to evaluate, not a claim that every combination has been tested. Check compatibility, permissions and current account requirements before adopting one.

Tool or resourceUseful forFirst useful test
ChatGPT Work Skill CreatorTurning a repeatable process into a skillGive @skill-creator one input and an accepted output.
Codex skills catalogFinding published skills for CodexRead the instructions and dependencies before installation.
Anthropic skills catalogStudying examples and creator workflowsInspect one relevant skill and its bundled files.
Claude Code skillsUsing skills in development workflowsTry a narrow project task in a disposable example.
Agent Skills specificationUnderstanding portable folder structureCheck name, description and supporting file paths.
MCP documentationUnderstanding connections to external systemsIdentify the exact read operation your workflow needs.

Three useful starter stacks

Meeting follow-up

Use your assistant, a meeting skill, pasted notes and an action-list template. Compare extracted actions against the notes. Add a document connection only if repeated copying becomes a demonstrated bottleneck. Keep sending separate from drafting.

Content from evidence

Use a source collection, a drafting skill and a claim-review checklist. Require a source for factual claims and label editorial interpretation. Test whether the workflow admits missing evidence. A fluent draft with unsupported claims fails the test.

Development review

Use a repository-aware assistant, a narrowly scoped review skill and the project’s existing checks. Give it the expected behavior, changed files and a realistic failure case. Review the diff and test results before merging. A skill’s presence is not evidence that checks ran.

A scorecard you can reuse

Score each candidate from zero to two on task fit, source quality, setup effort, review effort and repeatability: zero means unsuitable, one means usable with changes, two means ready for your trial. Record a reason beside each score. Treat fabricated facts, unreviewed executable code or unexplained permissions as unresolved issues even when the total score looks good.

Compare tools with the same input and acceptance checklist. Count correction time, not just response speed. Save the date, product, skill version, source files and output. Repeat after material changes. These are our suggested evaluation practices, not a vendor benchmark.

When to add another tool

Add a tool when you can name the missing capability: read a current document, calculate a deterministic value, render a file or update an approved record. MCP provides a standard connection mechanism; it does not itself supply your business rules, credentials or a schedule. Avoid building a large stack before your first workflow produces an acceptable result.

For a complete exercise with expected answers, difficult inputs and a seven-day practice plan, use the Wealth Experiment skill-building lab.

title: Steal my stack: give every AI tool a clear job
description: Borrow the workflow thinking behind seven online brands. Map the task, inputs, tools, handoffs, and human checkpoints before adding another app.
quickAnswer: Begin with one result you want to deliver. Map its inputs, steps, and review points, then assign tools to specific jobs. The seven-brand Steal My Stack map shows offers and possible revenue paths; it does not claim that every brand earns income or uses an identical setup.
author: Ashley Kays
bodyHtml:
I built seven online brands and mapped the offers, tools, and workflows behind them. Steal My Stack gives you a way to see how the pieces connect and choose a useful starting point of your own.

AI Superpower's part of the map is about choosing tools for work you can describe. What do you want to finish? What information does the tool need? What should the output contain? How will you know whether it is useful?

Answer those questions before choosing the next app. They give you a brief you can test and a reason for each tool you keep.

Map the job from input to finished result

Consider an illustrative task: turning approved notes into a useful offer page. The inputs might be an audience description, the actual deliverable, the price or scoping process, and evidence you have permission to share. The result is a page a prospective customer can understand and act on.

StageTool's jobHuman checkpoint
UnderstandOrganize supplied research and questions.Check the evidence, context, and missing facts.
CreateDraft copy or a page structure from the brief.Approve the offer, scope, and claims.
BuildHelp implement the approved page.Review the layout, links, mobile view, and actions.
DeliverSupport the agreed inquiry or purchase process.Verify the real confirmation and fulfillment.
ImproveOrganize observations and possible changes.Decide what the evidence supports and what to try next.

This is a workflow to adapt, not a report of measured performance. Start with a manual pass on permitted material. It helps expose missing information before you connect more systems.

Separate the tools from the offer

The customer chooses a useful result. The stack helps you produce and deliver it. A tool belongs in your workflow when you can name the job it does and the output the next step needs.

The wider map includes tools from my broader work alongside suggested workflows. It is not a requirement to subscribe to every tool or a claim that every brand runs the same integrations. A small project may need a document, a simple page, and a clear way to respond. More complex work may need application data, payments, or recurring automation.

Use your current setup first where it meets the need. Add a tool when you can identify a real gap, understand the cost and permissions, and check the result.

Write down the handoffs

Many workflow problems appear between steps. A research summary loses its source links. A draft adds an offer you have not approved. A form accepts a request but the person responsible never sees it.

For each handoff, record what is passed along, where it goes, who reviews it, and what happens if it fails. For a public page, keep the approved brief with the draft. For an inquiry, define the acknowledgement and owner. For a paid product, check the actual payment and delivery before describing the flow as complete.

Human checkpoints are especially useful where the work changes meaning: from an idea to a claim, a draft to a publication, or an inquiry to an agreed project. Give the reviewer enough context to make that decision.

Run a small, fair tool trial

  1. Choose one task you understand well enough to evaluate.
  2. Give each option the same permitted input and expected output.
  3. Review factual accuracy, completeness, usability, and the effort needed to correct it.
  4. Record subscription costs and any setup or integration work that matters.
  5. Keep the option that fits your task, or continue with your existing process if the trial does not improve it.

The Tool Trial Lab gives you a place to structure that comparison. If you are still deciding what to work on, start with a useful workflow and a sample task.

A reusable prompt for choosing your stack

My goal is [result]. My inputs are [materials]. My current tools are [tools]. My time and spending limits are [limits]. Map the steps from input to finished output. Assign each step a tool or a person. Identify missing information, handoffs, and review checkpoints. Start with tools I already have. Treat new integrations as proposals to check, and do not invent performance results or assume accounts are connected.

Review the suggested plan, complete one small pass, and save what you learned. A repeatable workflow should be understandable enough to hand to another person and flexible enough to change when the task changes.

How this brand can earn

AI Superpower offers free discovery and learning alongside working sessions, workflow setup, team training, and launch support. Tool makers can also inquire about clearly labeled promotion and newsletter partnerships. A sponsored placement does not buy a favorable review, and the existence of these offers does not establish sales.

These are different customer paths. A person choosing a tool can use the free workflows. A team needing help can discuss a scoped engagement. A maker can review the promotion terms and audience evidence before agreeing to a placement.

Explore the full Steal My Stack map or download the seven-brand PDF. Choose one result, map the work, and give each tool a clear job.

title: Give Claude five jobs on your next YouTube video
description: Use Claude to plan a YouTube video, develop titles and thumbnails, write editing briefs, organize review notes, and select useful clips with five reusable prompts.
quickAnswer: Give Claude a timestamped transcript and five separate roles: producer, packaging strategist, edit planner, clip selector, and reviewer. Keep final editorial decisions and video exports with a person and a video editor.
bodyHtml:
A useful recording contains decisions, examples, and experience that your audience can learn from. This workflow helps you turn that material into a clear video brief and a focused set of follow-up pieces.

Build a useful workflow with five clear roles

You can organize a practical AI video workflow around five roles: producer, title writer, editing assistant, review coordinator, and repurposing assistant. Each role receives specific inputs and produces something you can inspect.

Start with one conversation and run the roles in sequence. You do not need five separate agents to try this. Save the instructions that work, then consider a more automated setup only after you understand the handoffs.

This is a workflow and prompt guide. It does not install a video editor or claim that a standard chat can automatically cut, render, and publish your footage. Use your chosen editor for the actual cuts and exports. Additional execution depends on the tools you connect and test.

Prepare a small input pack

Begin with a timestamped transcript from your transcription or editing tool. Claude’s documented upload formats include text documents and still images, so a checked transcript and relevant screenshots are practical inputs. Check Claude’s current upload guidance for the formats supported in your account.

Add a short audience brief, the intended viewer action, your tone, approved facts, and any claims that need checking. Include examples of your own writing if you want the supporting copy to sound consistent.

  • Audience: who the video helps and what they already know.
  • Promise: the useful question the recording answers.
  • Evidence: demonstrations, verified facts, and approved examples.
  • Constraints: topics, claims, or material that must not be used.
  • Source: transcript version and recording filename.
  • Next action: the relevant destination or task for the viewer.

Remove confidential material you are not authorized to share. Check names, numbers, specialist terms, and speaker labels. If the transcript has no timestamps, ask for quotations and section references instead of allowing invented timecodes.

Role 1: producer — find the strongest useful promise

The producer’s job is to decide what the video is about and what belongs in it. Ask Claude to identify the central idea, the intended viewer, and the example that makes the explanation concrete.

Act as the planning producer for this video. Using only the brief and transcript, identify the intended viewer, the main question, the useful promise, and the strongest supporting example. Propose a clear section order. Mark material that repeats another point or belongs in a separate video. List missing context and claims that need verification. Do not add experiences, examples, or results that are absent from the source.

Review the proposed promise against the actual recording. If the transcript contains three unrelated themes, choose one or split the project. Do not make a title about the most exciting sentence if the rest of the video cannot support it.

What you keep: a one-page production brief with the audience, promise, sequence, evidence, next action, and open questions.

Role 2: title writer — develop three distinct concepts

Ask for different ways to communicate the same truthful promise. A diagnosis, a demonstration, and a misconception can produce meaningfully different concepts. You are choosing the reason the right viewer would watch.

Using the approved production brief and transcript, create three title and thumbnail concepts. For each, give a title, a simple visual description, optional short thumbnail text, the viewer question, and the source passage that supports the promise. Make the concepts distinct. Flag exaggeration, missing proof, or a need for additional footage. Do not claim guaranteed growth, secret access, or measured results unless the source establishes them.

Check the title in plain language. Does a person outside your team understand the subject? Can the thumbnail communicate at small size? Does the concept fit the audience you actually want?

What you keep: a shortlist for a designer or image tool to create. A thumbnail concept is a creative brief; inspect any resulting image for accuracy, legibility, and rights before publishing.

Role 3: editing assistant — prepare an actionable cut list

Give Claude the approved concept and ask for suggestions tied to the source. A useful brief distinguishes an editorial suggestion from something that requires a person to inspect the footage.

Prepare an editing brief for the approved video concept. Use only existing transcript timestamps. For each suggestion, provide the source range, action, reason, and any visual or audio check needed. Suggest a concise opening from available material, flag repetition, and identify where a demonstration would help. Preserve qualifications and the speaker’s meaning. If timestamps are missing, quote the passage instead. Do not claim that you have edited or watched footage you have not accessed.

Open the recording and verify each important suggestion. A transcript alone cannot assess facial expressions, camera focus, audio quality, or whether a proposed cut creates a jarring transition. Keep enough context for examples and qualifications to remain understandable.

What you keep: an edit brief the editor can act on. Preserve the original recording and produce a new version for each review round.

Role 4: review coordinator — turn feedback into clear actions

Review notes become more useful when they refer to a specific version and describe a concrete change. A shared sheet is sufficient for a first workflow; a timeline-commenting tool is optional.

Organize these review notes for video version [version]. Return a table with timestamp or source reference, requested change, reason, priority, owner, and status. Combine duplicates, flag contradictions, and identify notes that need clarification. Preserve the reviewer’s intent. Do not mark an item complete without evidence from the revised export or the responsible editor.

An illustrative note is: “Version 2, 00:20: move the short demonstration before the longer explanation.” When the editor changes the timeline, the old timestamp may no longer point to the same moment. Keep the version label attached.

What you keep: a consolidated review list and a clear record of who approves the final export. Watch that export yourself; a tidy checklist is not proof that the changes were applied correctly.

Role 5: repurposing assistant — choose excerpts worth sharing

Ask for a small shortlist of moments that communicate a complete idea. Review the selection for meaning before considering how attention-grabbing it is.

Find up to three excerpts that could work as standalone short videos. For each, give the source range or exact quotation, the viewer question, the takeaway, necessary context, and a suggested caption. Explain why it deserves a separate asset. Preserve qualifications and avoid fragments that could mislead. If fewer than three meet the standard, return fewer. Then adapt one approved lesson into a LinkedIn post and a short email without inventing first-person experiences.

Check that the clip has a beginning, a useful point, and an ending. Replace unclear references with a short introduction if the edit supports it. Keep the complete meaning when cropping and adding captions.

What you keep: selected source ranges, crop notes, checked captions, and separate written drafts for the channels you actually use.

Keep the workflow simple and inspect the handoffs

Use a folder for the source, a folder for working files, and a folder for approved exports. Maintain a small tracker with the asset, version, owner, status, and destination. A consistent naming convention prevents an old cut from becoming the published one.

Run each role as a separate pass and approve the output before it becomes the next role’s input. If the producer chooses an inaccurate promise, every later step can become polished around the wrong idea.

When evaluating a tool connection, check what it can read, what it can change, where outputs are saved, and how failed actions are reported. Begin with a duplicate or test project. Add automatic publishing only when the owner has authorized it and the final-review process is reliable.

Prompt tip: give the assistant permission to return “not enough evidence” or fewer recommendations. Requiring a fixed number of impressive ideas encourages filler.

Check the result before increasing volume

Run the workflow on one recording. Record how long preparation, editing, review, and corrections take. Note repeated failures such as invented timestamps, inaccurate captions, or titles that overpromise.

After publication, compare the audience response with relevant previous work and look for useful customer actions. Treat AI’s explanation of performance as a hypothesis to check. The point of the first trial is to learn whether the process produces useful, accurate work at a sustainable cost.

  • The title and thumbnail match the approved lesson.
  • Every cut and quotation preserves meaning.
  • The final export has been watched and heard.
  • Captions, mobile crops, and destination links work.
  • Rights and permissions for footage, music, and customer material are clear.
  • The published file is the approved version.

Save the prompts you actually found useful and revise them when a recurring problem appears. To make the evaluation concrete, plan a useful tool trial around one recording and one clear review standard.
